title: Integer division into a double
summary: Why division can lose its fractional part before the answer reaches a double, and how to get the decimal result you expect.
objectives: Explain why dividing two `int` values discards the fractional part, even when the result is stored in a `double`.
Trace the types and values in an integer division expression.
Fix integer division by making at least one operand a floating-point value before division.
Recognize the same mistake in averages, fractions and casts.

blocks.text: A `double` can hold a decimal value. But putting an integer division result into a `double` does not bring back a fraction that was already discarded. This program compiles, but prints `0.0` instead of the expected `0.5`.

bad.title: The division happens as integer division

good.title: Make an operand a double first

blocks.note: Both versions compile without a warning. In the first, `sum` and `count` are both `int`, so `sum / count` gives the integer result `0`. Java then stores that `0` in `average` as `0.0`. In the second, `(double) sum` makes the division use a floating-point value, so the result is `0.5`.

blocks.text: Java chooses how division works from the types of the values being divided. When both operands are `int`, the result is an `int`. Java discards the fractional part; it does not round. The type of the variable receiving the answer does not change how the division was done.

blocks.caption: What happens when two int values are divided and the answer goes into a double

blocks.caption: Integer division discards the fraction; floating-point division keeps it

series.name: At least one operand is double

blocks.title: Change the division, not just the destination
blocks.text: For a decimal answer, make at least one operand a floating-point value before division. For example, write `7.0 / 2` or `(double) sum / count`.

sections.title: Trace it one step at a time

blocks.text: Follow the expression from its operands to the variable that receives the answer. This makes it clear why the `double` does not rescue the fraction.

blocks.caption: Tracing `double average = sum / count;` when `sum` is 1 and `count` is 2
rows: Both operands are `int`, so integer division gives `0`

blocks.text: The important step is step 3: the division has already produced `0`. Assignment changes how that value is stored, not how it was calculated. With `(double) sum / count`, the first operand is a `double`, so the division produces `0.5` instead.
In each example, ask what types the operands have at the moment `/` runs. That tells you whether Java keeps the fraction.

bad.title: A double destination does not fix 7 / 2

good.title: A double operand keeps the fraction

blocks.note: In the first program, `7` and `2` are both `int`, so `7 / 2` gives `3` before it is stored as `3.0`. In the second, `7.0` is a `double`, so division keeps the fractional part and gives `3.5`.

bad.title: Cast after the division: the fraction is already gone

good.title: Cast before the division

blocks.note: In the first program, the parentheses make `1 / 4` happen first. Both values are `int`, so that gives `0`; casting that result makes it `0.0`. In the second, `(double) 1` makes one operand a `double` before `/` runs.

blocks.text: The mistake can hide in an average, a fraction or any calculation whose result is meant to be decimal. These short examples are code fragments, not complete programs.

bad.title: Average of two integers loses a fraction

good.title: Make the division use a double

blocks.note: If `a` and `b` are `int`, then `(a + b) / 2` uses integer division. Casting the sum before `/` lets an average such as `1.5` stay decimal.

bad.title: A fraction assigned to double still becomes zero

blocks.note: The first line compiles, but the division is between two `int` values, so `quarter` becomes `0.0`. The second line uses a `double` operand and gives `0.25`.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
blocks.explanation: `9` and `10` are both `int`, so `9 / 10` gives `0` and discards the fraction. That value is then stored as `0.0` in `result`. The code compiles.

blocks.question: Which expression makes the division keep its fractional part?
blocks.explanation: `1.0` is a `double`, so at least one operand is floating-point when `/` runs. The other expressions divide two `int` values first, or explicitly use `int`.

blocks.question: What does this expression produce?
blocks.explanation: The cast makes `7` a `double` before division. The division therefore keeps the fraction and produces `3.5`.

items: When both operands of `/` are `int`, Java discards the fractional part. It does not round.
The result of `int` division is decided before assignment. A `double` destination cannot restore a discarded fraction.
To get a decimal result, make at least one operand a floating-point value before division, as in `7.0 / 2`.
A cast must happen before the division: `(double) sum / count` works; `(double) (sum / count)` casts after.
This mistake compiles. Trace the operand types at `/` to catch it before running the program.
